The integration module is not about learning new findings — it is about synthesizing the findings from Modules 1–5 into a coherent hemodynamic picture that drives a management decision. Bedside echo in the ICU is not a diagnostic test. It is a clinical tool for real-time hemodynamic characterization and therapeutic guidance.

section: 2. The four-question bedside echo in shock
text:
2. The four-question bedside echo in shock
A systematic framework for the undifferentiated hemodynamically unstable patient.
Every bedside echo in shock should answer these four questions, in this order:
1. Is there a pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology? If yes, stop — this is the diagnosis and the intervention is pericardiocentesis. Do not proceed with a hemodynamic workup until tamponade is excluded or treated.
2. What is LV systolic function? Severely reduced = cardiogenic component. Hyperdynamic = distributive or hypovolemic. Normal requires further assessment.
3. What is RV size and function? Dilated RV with D-sign and a normal or hyperdynamic LV = obstructive physiology (PE) or acute cor pulmonale until proven otherwise. RV dilation with reduced LV function = biventricular failure.
4. What is the IVC? Small and collapsible = low filling pressure, possible fluid responsiveness. Large and non-collapsing = elevated filling pressure, fluid loading is unlikely to help.






Tip



Video slot: Demonstration of a systematic 4-question exam — subcostal (pericardium + IVC), PLAX (LV + pericardium), PSAX (D-sign, LV function), apical 4-chamber (RV:LV ratio, LV wall motion).

title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
4. When findings conflict
The exam doesn’t always give you a clean answer.






Tip



Video slot: Mixed shock state — reduced EF with small IVC; how to interpret and what to do.


Common conflicting scenarios and how to reason through them:
Reduced EF + small IVC The LV is failing but filling pressures are low — the patient is hypovolemic relative to their baseline. A cautious fluid trial (250 mL) may improve preload and cardiac output without tipping into pulmonary edema. Monitor closely.
Hyperdynamic LV + plethoric IVC High-output state with elevated venous pressure. Consider: severe sepsis with right heart congestion, severe tricuspid regurgitation, hepatic disease, or a patient in compensated high-output heart failure who has been aggressively fluid-loaded.
Normal LV + dilated RV + plethoric IVC (no effusion) Obstructive physiology from PE or acute cor pulmonale from ARDS. Do not give more fluid. Focus on diagnosis and afterload reduction.
Large effusion + no tamponade physiology + plethoric IVC Consider chronic effusion (malignant, uremic) with concomitant right heart failure causing the elevated IVC — these are two separate problems. Treat both.

title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
5. Serial exams and trending
Echo is not a one-time test.






Tip



Video slot: Before/after comparison — echo before and after 1 L fluid bolus in a patient with septic shock.


The true power of bedside echo in critical care is the ability to perform serial exams and track the response to interventions in real time. Key scenarios for repeat assessment:

After a fluid bolus: Did IVC diameter change? Did cardiac output improve (visual or measured)? Did venous congestion worsen?
After vasopressor dose change: Did LV or RV filling improve?
After diuresis: Is venous congestion resolving? Is IVC size decreasing?
After pericardiocentesis: Is tamponade physiology resolved? Is there residual constrictive physiology?
Trending over hours: Is RV function improving with treatment of PE or ARDS? Is EF recovering in myocarditis?

Each exam should be compared to the prior exam, not interpreted in isolation. Document the key findings (EF category, RV:LV ratio, IVC diameter, IVC collapsibility) so that trends are visible across shifts.

title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
6. Integration cases
Complex cases requiring synthesis of all modules.


Case 1: The patient in undifferentiated shock
Clinical scenario: A 64-year-old man with no significant cardiac history is transferred from a community hospital with “septic shock, possible PE.” He has been on norepinephrine for 6 hours and received 5 L of crystalloid. On arrival: BP 74/48, HR 128, temp 37.8°C, O2 sat 90% on 6 L NC. He is slightly confused. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. Troponin is mildly elevated.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation — complete four-window exam.


What you see: 1. No pericardial effusion. 2. LV severely reduced EF. Global hypokinesis, no RWMA. 3. RV moderately dilated. D-sign present. McConnell’s sign absent. TAPSE 14 mm. 4. IVC 2.5 cm, non-collapsing.
Integration: This is not simple septic shock. The severely reduced LV EF with RV dilation and a plethoric IVC suggests biventricular failure. The bilateral infiltrates could reflect pulmonary edema rather than pneumonia. The elevated troponin is consistent with cardiogenic shock. The differential includes new dilated cardiomyopathy with acute decompensation, fulminant myocarditis, or sepsis-induced biventricular dysfunction.
How does this change management? Stop fluids — the patient is congested. Add dobutamine for inotropic support. Get a 12-lead ECG and urgent formal echo. Consider PA catheter to characterize hemodynamics. The “sepsis” label may be wrong — treat aggressively for a primary cardiac event. If troponin is significantly elevated and ECG shows ischemic changes, activate the cath lab.



Case 2: Post-arrest resuscitation — what caused the arrest?
Clinical scenario: A 58-year-old woman had a witnessed cardiac arrest in the hospital corridor. She was resuscitated in 8 minutes with 2 shocks and CPR. Now intubated, hemodynamically marginal on vasopressors. No prior cardiac history. The team wants to know: VF arrest from ACS, PE, or something else?
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: 1. No effusion. 2. LV: anterior and apical wall akinesis. Severely reduced EF. No global hypokinesis — the inferior and lateral walls move. 3. RV: normal size. No D-sign. Normal TAPSE. 4. IVC: 2.0 cm, 30% collapse (borderline).
Integration: Regional wall motion abnormality in the anterior/LAD distribution with a normal RV. This is a large anterior STEMI causing VF arrest. The RV is not dilated — this is not a PE causing the arrest. The IVC is borderline, consistent with post-resuscitation state.
How does this change management? Activate the cath lab immediately for emergent PCI. This is STEMI-equivalent post-arrest — coronary angiography is indicated regardless of the post-resuscitation ECG. Initiate targeted temperature management per protocol. The echo finding of an anterior RWMA pointing to the LAD is the critical finding that directs the team to the right intervention.



Case 3: Hypoxic respiratory failure — cardiac or pulmonary?
Clinical scenario: A 71-year-old woman with COPD is admitted with progressive dyspnea over 3 days. She is hypoxic (O2 sat 84% on 10 L), hypotensive (BP 90/60), and has bilateral crackles and lower extremity edema. BNP is 1,800 pg/mL. Chest X-ray shows bilateral opacities. The team is debating whether to intubate for COPD exacerbation or initiate diuresis for decompensated heart failure.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: 1. No effusion. 2. LV: severely reduced EF, dilated — chronic appearance. 3. RV: moderately dilated. D-sign (diastolic flattening, consistent with volume overload). 4. IVC: 2.8 cm, non-collapsing. Hepatic veins dilated.
Integration: Decompensated heart failure with reduced EF, biventricular volume overload, and severe congestion — not a primary COPD exacerbation. The COPD may be contributing to increased RV afterload, but the dominant pathophysiology is cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
How does this change management? Initiate NIV (BiPAP) to reduce preload and work of breathing. Begin aggressive diuresis. Add dobutamine if hemodynamics do not improve with afterload and preload reduction. Do not intubate for COPD management — the indication, if intubation becomes necessary, is respiratory failure from cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Treat the heart.



Case 4: The patient who “isn’t responding” to treatment
Clinical scenario: A 77-year-old man with known COPD and newly diagnosed lung cancer was admitted 3 days ago for presumed COPD exacerbation. He has been on bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics with minimal improvement. He remains hypoxic and increasingly vasopressor-dependent. Repeat echo is requested by the ICU attending.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: 1. Moderate pericardial effusion. No RA or RV collapse. IVC plethoric. 2. LV: normal EF. No RWMA. 3. RV: moderately dilated. D-sign present (pressure overload pattern — systolic flattening). 4. IVC: 2.4 cm, non-collapsing.
Integration: Two separate findings: a pericardial effusion (likely malignant) and RV pressure overload without tamponade physiology. The effusion is not causing tamponade. The RV dilation with pressure-overload D-sign in a patient with lung cancer raises the possibility of pulmonary hypertension from tumor invasion, PE, or extrinsic pulmonary vascular compression. Neither finding fits a primary COPD exacerbation.
How does this change management? CT pulmonary angiography to evaluate for PE and pulmonary vascular involvement by tumor. Oncology consultation for the effusion (malignant pericardial effusion likely). Reframe the clinical diagnosis — this is not a COPD exacerbation. The failure to respond to bronchodilators and steroids was a clue that the diagnosis was wrong.



Case 5: The post-operative patient who won’t come off the ventilator
Clinical scenario: A 69-year-old man undergoes elective aortic valve replacement. He is extubated on post-op day 2 but reintubated 6 hours later for respiratory failure. He is now post-op day 5, sedated, and failing repeated extubation trials. An ICU team requests bedside echo to evaluate hemodynamics.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation — post-surgical windows (often challenging).


What you see: 1. Small anterior effusion. No chamber collapse. 2. LV: EF 45% (mildly reduced, new compared to pre-op 60%). Anterior wall motion mildly reduced. 3. RV: mildly dilated. TAPSE 14 mm. 4. IVC: 2.2 cm, 20% distensibility (borderline for fluid responsiveness in a ventilated patient).
Integration: New mild LV dysfunction (post-operative stunned myocardium vs perioperative MI), mild RV dysfunction, and borderline volume status. The anterior wall motion abnormality raises concern for a perioperative LAD event. The ventricular dysfunction is driving respiratory failure — the patient is not failing extubation from pulmonary mechanics but from hemodynamic compromise.
How does this change management? Obtain an ECG and serial troponins — a perioperative MI must be ruled out. Cardiology consultation for post-surgical echo. Optimize hemodynamics: gentle diuresis to reduce preload, optimize heart rate, consider low-dose inotrope if EF remains depressed. Address the cardiac problem before the next extubation trial — the respiratory failure is a symptom, not the diagnosis.






Tip



Integration reminder: The power of the four-question exam is not in any single finding. It is in the composite picture and the management decision that follows.

Quiz

Note



Q1. A patient in shock has a hyperdynamic LV, a dilated RV with D-sign, and a plethoric IVC. No pericardial effusion. What is the most likely hemodynamic phenotype and the priority intervention?






Caution





Answer Obstructive shock from pulmonary embolism (or acute cor pulmonale). The hyperdynamic LV is underfilled due to RV failure impairing output. The priority is reducing RV afterload — systemic anticoagulation, and in hemodynamic collapse, systemic thrombolytics or catheter-directed therapy. Do not give fluid boluses.



Q2. You find a severely reduced EF and a small, collapsible IVC in a hypotensive patient. What does this suggest and how do you manage it?






Caution





Answer The LV is failing but filling pressures are low — cardiogenic shock superimposed on hypovolemia (or volume depletion from prior diuresis/bleeding). A cautious fluid challenge (250 mL) may improve preload and cardiac output. Monitor closely for pulmonary edema. Add inotropic support if the EF does not improve with preload optimization.



Q3. After performing a bedside echo, you are unsure whether the reduced EF is new or chronic. How does the LV size help you distinguish?






Caution





Answer A dilated LV suggests a chronic process — the heart has had time to remodel. A non-dilated LV with severely reduced EF suggests an acute process (myocarditis, Takotsubo, acute MI, sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy). Acuity changes the differential and the urgency of investigation (e.g., emergent cath lab for suspected acute MI vs. supportive management for myocarditis).



Q4. A patient’s echo shows: no effusion, normal LV, dilated RV with McConnell’s sign, plethoric IVC. What is the diagnosis and what is the single most important intervention?






Caution





Answer Massive pulmonary embolism with RV failure. The single most important intervention is systemic thrombolysis (if no contraindication) — it rapidly reduces RV afterload by dissolving the clot. Anticoagulation alone is insufficient in hemodynamic collapse. Activate a PE response team or get interventional radiology and cardiac surgery on the line simultaneously.



Q5. What is the purpose of serial bedside echo in the ICU, and what should be documented to make serial exams useful?






Caution





Answer Serial echo tracks the response to interventions and identifies deterioration or recovery over time. A single exam is a snapshot; serial exams reveal trajectory. Document key quantitative or semi-quantitative findings at each exam: EF category (severely reduced / mildly reduced / normal / hyperdynamic), RV:LV ratio, IVC diameter and collapsibility, presence of chamber collapse or D-sign. This allows any clinician picking up the patient to immediately understand where the hemodynamics started and where they are now.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Two questions beyond the basics covered in Module 1.

Is this pericarditis, and is there an effusion that requires intervention? The diagnosis of acute pericarditis is primarily clinical (pleuritic chest pain, friction rub, ECG changes), but echo defines the effusion, tracks its size, and identifies patients at highest risk of progression to tamponade.
Is this constrictive pericarditis? Constriction is the great mimic of right heart failure and the one pericardial diagnosis that requires surgical intervention. It is frequently missed on bedside echo but there are clues — knowing what to look for can prompt the right specialist consultation.



This module builds on the effusion and tamponade content from Module 1. The focus here is on the clinical syndromes that follow pericardial injury — acute pericarditis, recurrent pericarditis, effusive-constrictive disease, and constrictive pericarditis — and on the more nuanced echo features that inform risk stratification and referral.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
The acquisition technique for pericardial assessment is the same as covered in Module 1 (subcostal, PLAX, apical four-chamber). This module adds targeted assessment for constrictive physiology, which requires Doppler interrogation beyond standard 2D imaging.


Mitral inflow — pulsed wave Doppler






Tip



Video slot: PW Doppler at mitral valve tips — E/A ratio, respiratory variation in constriction vs normal.


Probe: Phased array, apical four-chamber. Sample volume at the tips of the mitral valve leaflets. Assess E-wave and A-wave velocity and their variation with respiration.
What you are looking for: In constrictive pericarditis, mitral E-wave velocity decreases by more than 25% with inspiration (the opposite of what happens in normal physiology). This is the Doppler equivalent of pulsus paradoxus and reflects exaggerated interventricular dependence due to the rigid pericardial shell.



Tricuspid inflow — pulsed wave Doppler






Tip



Video slot: PW Doppler at tricuspid valve tips — reciprocal respiratory variation (increases with inspiration in constriction).


What you are looking for: In constriction, as mitral E-wave falls with inspiration, tricuspid E-wave rises reciprocally. This exaggerated and reciprocal respiratory variation across the AV valves is the hallmark of constrictive physiology.



Hepatic vein flow — pulsed wave Doppler






Tip



Video slot: Hepatic vein PW Doppler — expiratory diastolic flow reversal in constriction.


What you are looking for: In constriction, diastolic flow reversal in the hepatic veins is prominent with expiration (opposite of restrictive cardiomyopathy, where reversal is with inspiration). This finding, combined with the AV valve respiratory variation, is highly specific for constrictive pericarditis.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
3. Normal & normal variants

Normal pericardium on 2D
As reviewed in Module 1: thin, bright echogenic line, no echo-free space between layers, moves with the heart. A normal pericardium on 2D does not rule out constrictive pericarditis — the thickened, calcified pericardium of constriction is visible in only a subset of cases on standard echo.


Normal mitral inflow Doppler
E/A ratio 0.8–1.5 in normal adults. Mild respiratory variation (<25%) is normal. The E-wave represents early passive filling; the A-wave represents atrial contraction. Both should be present in sinus rhythm.


Normal hepatic vein flow
Predominantly anterograde systolic and diastolic flow toward the heart, with minor physiologic reversal at end-systole. Marked diastolic flow reversal is not normal.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding, not by diagnosis.

Acute pericarditis with effusion






Tip



Video slot: Small-to-moderate effusion in the context of pericarditis — preserved function, no tamponade physiology.


Acute pericarditis is an inflammatory syndrome. Echo is used to characterize and track the effusion, not to make the diagnosis (which is clinical). Most effusions in acute pericarditis are small and do not require drainage.
Risk features that warrant closer monitoring and possible hospitalization:

Large effusion (>2 cm)
Tamponade physiology (see Module 1)
Fever >38°C with subacute onset
Immunocompromised state
Anticoagulation (risk of hemopericardium)
Failure to respond to NSAIDs within 1 week

Teaching points:

A normal echo does not rule out acute pericarditis.
Colchicine reduces recurrence and should be added to NSAIDs in all cases without contraindication.
Serial echo at 1 week to assess effusion trajectory is appropriate when an effusion is present at diagnosis.




Myopericarditis






Tip



Video slot: Pericarditis with regional or global LV dysfunction — the myopericarditis overlap syndrome.


When myocardial inflammation accompanies pericarditis, LV function may be impaired. This is more common than recognized and ranges from subtle wall motion abnormality to frank cardiomyopathy.
Teaching points:

Any patient with pericarditis and an elevated troponin should have LV function assessed by echo.
Regional wall motion abnormalities suggest myocardial involvement, not just pericardial.
Activity restriction is prolonged in myopericarditis (3–6 months vs 2–4 weeks for isolated pericarditis).
NSAIDs may be harmful if significant myocarditis is present — cardiology consultation is warranted.




Effusive-constrictive pericarditis






Tip



Video slot: Effusion with constrictive physiology — persistence of elevated filling pressures after pericardiocentesis.


A syndrome where both effusion and constrictive pericardial thickening coexist. The effusion may be the dominant finding initially, but after drainage, elevated filling pressures and constrictive Doppler features persist.
Teaching points:

Suspect this diagnosis when a patient fails to improve hemodynamically after pericardiocentesis.
Common causes: tuberculosis, radiation-induced pericardial disease, malignancy.
Requires formal echo with Doppler after drainage to identify residual constriction.
May ultimately require pericardiectomy.




Constrictive pericarditis






Tip



Video slots: - Septal bounce on M-mode or 2D — the abrupt early diastolic septal shift - Respiratory variation on mitral inflow (>25% E-wave decrease with inspiration) - Reciprocal tricuspid inflow increase with inspiration - Expiratory hepatic vein diastolic flow reversal


Constrictive pericarditis results from a thickened, fibrotic, or calcified pericardium that limits diastolic filling. It is the great mimic of right heart failure, liver disease, and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Key 2D features:

Pericardial thickening or calcification (may not be visible on echo; CT is more sensitive)
Septal bounce — an abrupt early diastolic shift of the interventricular septum, reflecting exaggerated ventricular interdependence
Normal or mildly elevated RVSP (unlike restrictive CMP, where PA pressures are often markedly elevated)
Dilated IVC and hepatic veins (elevated venous pressure)

Key Doppler features:

Mitral E-wave decrease >25% with inspiration
Reciprocal tricuspid E-wave increase with inspiration
Expiratory diastolic flow reversal in hepatic veins

Constriction is surgically curable — pericardiectomy — but carries significant operative risk. Early identification and referral to a center with expertise matters.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Recurrent chest pain after pericarditis
Clinical scenario: A 35-year-old man had an episode of acute pericarditis 3 months ago, treated with NSAIDs. He now returns with recurrent pleuritic chest pain and low-grade fever. His prior echo showed a small effusion that had resolved at his 4-week follow-up.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for recurrent effusion and LV function.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Small effusion, posterior. No tamponade physiology. Normal LV function.
How does this change management? Recurrent pericarditis with small effusion. No high-risk features. Restart NSAIDs and colchicine. If not already on colchicine, prescribe it now — it halves the recurrence rate. Cardiology consultation for refractory recurrent pericarditis (consider IL-1 inhibitor therapy such as anakinra or rilonacept if this is the second or third recurrence).



Case 2: Progressive dyspnea after radiation therapy
Clinical scenario: A 58-year-old woman with a history of mediastinal radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma 15 years ago presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, lower extremity edema, and ascites. JVD is present. Echo from her oncologist 2 years ago reportedly showed “normal function.”
What exam would you perform? Comprehensive focused cardiac ultrasound including Doppler interrogation of mitral and tricuspid inflows and hepatic veins.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Normal LV size and function. RV mildly dilated. Septal bounce visible. Plethoric IVC and hepatic veins. Mitral E-wave decreases >30% with inspiration. Expiratory diastolic flow reversal in hepatic veins.
How does this change management? Constrictive pericarditis from radiation-induced pericardial disease. This is surgically curable. Refer to cardiothoracic surgery for pericardiectomy evaluation. Formal echo and cardiac catheterization (to confirm equalization of diastolic pressures) will be required. Treat symptoms with diuresis as a bridge. This diagnosis has been present for years — the prior echo likely had sufficient Doppler data if it had been obtained.



Case 3: Post-pericardiocentesis hemodynamic instability
Clinical scenario: A 64-year-old man with tuberculosis-associated pericardial effusion underwent pericardiocentesis yesterday with drainage of 700 mL. Today he remains hypotensive (BP 86/58) and volume-overloaded, with persistent JVD and edema.
What exam would you perform? Repeat focused cardiac ultrasound with Doppler.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Residual small effusion. Persistent plethoric IVC. Septal bounce. Mitral E-wave respiratory variation >25%.
How does this change management? Effusive-constrictive pericarditis — the effusion was not the only problem. Constrictive physiology persists after drainage, consistent with TB-related pericardial fibrosis. Cardiothoracic surgery consultation for pericardiectomy evaluation. Continue anti-tubercular therapy. The diagnosis of effusive-constrictive disease changes the expectation: this patient will not normalize with drainage alone.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. What are the high-risk features in acute pericarditis that warrant hospitalization?






Caution





Answer Large effusion (>2 cm), tamponade physiology, fever >38°C with subacute onset, immunocompromised state, anticoagulation therapy, failure to respond to NSAIDs within 1 week, and evidence of myocardial involvement (elevated troponin, RWMA).



Q2. What is the septal bounce, and what does it indicate?






Caution





Answer The septal bounce (also called the septal “shudder” or diastolic septal shift) is an abrupt early diastolic shift of the interventricular septum visible on 2D echo or M-mode. It reflects exaggerated ventricular interdependence due to the rigid pericardial shell — as the ventricles compete for a fixed intrapericardial volume, septal position shifts abruptly with respiration and filling. It is a key 2D sign of constrictive pericarditis.



Q3. How does the respiratory variation pattern on mitral inflow differ between constrictive pericarditis and cardiac tamponade?






Caution





Answer Both show exaggerated respiratory variation on mitral inflow (>25% E-wave decrease with inspiration). The distinction: in tamponade, the effusion is visible and chamber collapse is the primary finding. In constriction, there may be little or no effusion — the finding is the Doppler pattern and septal bounce, not the fluid. Constrictive physiology is a diagnosis of the pericardium’s mechanical behavior, not its fluid content.



Q4. A patient has features of right heart failure (JVD, edema, ascites, elevated JVP) but normal LV function and only modestly elevated PA pressure. What diagnosis should be high on the differential?






Caution





Answer Constrictive pericarditis. The combination of elevated venous pressure, normal LV function, and near-normal PA pressure is classic for constriction — in restrictive cardiomyopathy, PA pressures are typically more elevated. Other clues: history of prior pericarditis, cardiac surgery, radiation, or TB. A septal bounce and exaggerated mitral inflow respiratory variation support the diagnosis.



Q5. A patient undergoes pericardiocentesis for a large effusion and drains 600 mL. His hemodynamics do not improve. What should you consider?






Caution





Answer Effusive-constrictive pericarditis. The effusion was not the sole cause of hemodynamic compromise — constrictive physiology from underlying pericardial thickening or fibrosis persists after drainage. Repeat Doppler assessment post-drainage will show persistent elevated filling pressures and respiratory variation. This is common in TB-related and radiation-related pericardial disease and ultimately may require pericardiectomy.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Two questions in order.

Is global LV systolic function normal, reduced, or hyperdynamic? A visual estimate of ejection fraction — severely reduced, mildly-to-moderately reduced, normal, or hyperdynamic — is sufficient for bedside decision-making. You do not need a number.
Are there regional wall motion abnormalities? Segmental dysfunction in a coronary distribution suggests ACS as the etiology. Global dysfunction is more consistent with cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, or sepsis-mediated depression. The distinction changes management immediately.



Bedside LV assessment answers the most fundamental question in hemodynamic resuscitation: is the pump failing? A hypotensive patient with a hyperdynamic LV does not need inotropes — they need volume, vasopressors, or treatment of the underlying distributive state. A hypotensive patient with a severely reduced EF and dilated LV is in cardiogenic shock and needs a fundamentally different approach. Getting this wrong early leads to fluid overload in cardiogenic shock or undertreated distributive shock.

text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a phased array (cardiac) probe on the cardiac preset. LV function is assessed across multiple windows — no single view is sufficient. The goal is to visualize the LV in two orthogonal planes and assess wall motion in all segments.


Parasternal long axis






Tip



Video slot: PLAX for LV assessment — M-mode placement at mitral valve tips, visual EF estimation, posterior wall and septal motion.


What you are looking for: Global LV contractility (do the walls move vigorously inward in systole?), chamber size (a dilated LV suggests chronicity), and mitral valve excursion (reduced in low-output states). M-mode at the tips of the mitral valve leaflets allows measurement of EPSS (E-point septal separation) — a distance greater than 7 mm suggests reduced EF.



Parasternal short axis — papillary muscle level






Tip



Video slot: PSAX at papillary muscle level — the “donut” view, eyeball EF, D-sign assessment.


What you are looking for: The LV should appear round in cross-section and contract concentrically and symmetrically. This is the best single view for a visual EF estimate — watch the endocardium sweep inward in systole. Also assess the interventricular septum: a flat or D-shaped LV indicates RV pressure or volume overload (see Module 3).



Apical four-chamber






Tip



Video slot: Apical four-chamber for wall motion — septal, lateral, apical segments.


What you are looking for: All four chambers, with attention to LV wall motion in each visible segment. The apical view is essential for identifying apical wall motion abnormalities (LAD territory) and for assessing LV size relative to the RV.



Subcostal






Tip



Video slot: Subcostal cardiac view — rapid global LV assessment in the undifferentiated patient.


When to use: First-line in the unstable patient who cannot be repositioned. Provides a rapid visual impression of global LV function. Not sufficient alone for wall motion analysis.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
3. Normal & normal variants
The library of normal hearts and common confounders.






Tip



Video slots: Normal LV function across body habitus — thin patient, obese patient, patient with LVH. Review before the pathology library.



Normal LV systolic function
Normal EF is 55–70%. On visual assessment, the endocardial walls should move briskly inward in systole and the LV cavity should appear to nearly obliterate at peak contraction. The posterior wall and septum thicken in systole. A normal study looks vigorous — if you are unsure whether the function is normal, it probably is.


Hyperdynamic LV
EF greater than 70%, often with near-complete cavity obliteration in systole. Common in sepsis (early), anemia, hyperthyroidism, and hypovolemia. The hyperdynamic LV in a hypotensive patient points away from cardiogenic shock as the primary etiology — though it does not rule out mixed shock states.


LV hypertrophy
Increased wall thickness (septum or posterior wall >11 mm). Concentric hypertrophy (thick walls, normal cavity size) is seen in chronic hypertension and aortic stenosis. Eccentric hypertrophy (thick walls with a dilated cavity) suggests chronic volume overload. Hypertrophied ventricles are at higher risk for diastolic dysfunction and may decompensate with tachycardia or aggressive fluid loading.


“Kissing walls” in hypovolemia
In severe hypovolemia, the LV cavity may appear nearly obliterated even in diastole, with the walls nearly touching. This is distinct from a true reduction in EF — function appears hyperdynamic, not depressed. Seen in hemorrhagic shock, third-spacing, and aggressive diuresis.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding, not by diagnosis.

Severely reduced EF






Tip



Video slot: Severely reduced EF — dilated LV, minimal wall motion, large end-systolic volume.


EF visually estimated below 30%. The LV is often dilated. Wall motion is globally reduced with minimal inward thickening in systole. The mitral valve opens sluggishly and EPSS is markedly increased.
Teaching points:

This is cardiogenic shock physiology until proven otherwise in a hypotensive patient.
Causes: ischemic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, Takotsubo, sepsis-mediated depression (usually less severe).
Avoid aggressive fluid loading — the failing LV cannot handle preload augmentation and you will worsen pulmonary edema.
Inotropes (dobutamine) and early consideration of mechanical circulatory support are the interventions.




Mildly to moderately reduced EF






Tip



Video slot: Moderately reduced EF — reduced but present wall motion, mildly dilated LV.


EF visually estimated 30–50%. Wall motion is reduced but clearly present. The LV may or may not be dilated. This pattern is common in known heart failure with reduced EF presenting with decompensation.
Teaching points:

Does not automatically mean cardiogenic shock — assess for hemodynamic compromise and end-organ perfusion.
Treat the precipitant: arrhythmia, ischemia, infection, medication non-compliance, dietary indiscretion.
Avoid negative inotropes and large fluid boluses.




Regional wall motion abnormalities






Tip



Video slots: - Anterior RWMA (LAD territory) — apical and anterior wall hypokinesis - Inferior RWMA (RCA territory) — inferior and posterior wall hypokinesis - Lateral RWMA (LCx territory) — lateral wall hypokinesis


Segmental dysfunction confined to a coronary distribution. The affected wall moves less than adjacent segments or is akinetic (no motion) or dyskinetic (paradoxical outward motion in systole).
Teaching points:

New RWMA with hemodynamic compromise = acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. Activate the cath lab.
Assess the RV when inferior RWMA is present — RCA occlusion may cause concomitant RV infarct, which requires different management (avoid nitrates, volume-load to maintain RV preload).
Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy: apical ballooning with preserved or hyperdynamic basal segments — does not follow a coronary distribution. History of emotional or physiologic stressor.




Dilated LV






Tip



Video slot: Dilated LV — increased end-diastolic dimension, loss of the normal elliptical shape.


LV end-diastolic diameter greater than 5.5 cm (PLAX, M-mode) or a visually enlarged chamber. Dilation suggests chronicity — the heart has had time to remodel.
Teaching points:

A dilated LV with severely reduced EF is a chronic dilated cardiomyopathy. This patient likely has known disease and has decompensated.
A non-dilated LV with reduced EF suggests an acute process (myocarditis, Takotsubo, acute MI).
The distinction matters for prognosis and for anticipating how the LV will respond to treatment.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Hypotension after STEMI
Clinical scenario: A 61-year-old man with an anterior STEMI is brought to the ED. He received aspirin and heparin in the field. On arrival his BP is 78/50, HR 110, and he is cool and diaphoretic. The cath lab team is being activated.
What exam would you perform? Rapid focused cardiac ultrasound before transfer to the cath lab.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Severely reduced EF. Anterior and apical wall akinesis. LV not markedly dilated (acute presentation). No pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? This is cardiogenic shock from a large anterior MI. Start dobutamine at low dose as a bridge. Avoid aggressive fluid boluses. Notify the cath lab of cardiogenic shock — they may want an IABP or Impella placed at the time of PCI. Do not delay transfer for a prolonged echo.



Case 2: Undifferentiated hypotension in the ICU
Clinical scenario: A 58-year-old woman with septic shock from a urinary source has been on norepinephrine for 18 hours. She received 4 L of crystalloid. Her BP is now 72/40 despite escalating vasopressors. Lactate is rising.
What exam would you perform? Bedside cardiac ultrasound — LV function, RV size, IVC.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Severely reduced EF. Global hypokinesis. LV not dilated. IVC is plethoric.
How does this change management? This is sepsis-mediated cardiomyopathy with cardiogenic component to the shock. Add dobutamine. Stop or slow fluid administration. Consider PA catheter or advanced hemodynamic monitoring. Avoid further escalation of vasopressors alone — you are vasoconstricting a failing heart. Reassess in 4–6 hours; sepsis-mediated depression often recovers with treatment of the underlying infection.



Case 3: Chest pain and new ECG changes
Clinical scenario: A 49-year-old woman presents with 2 hours of substernal chest pressure and diaphoresis. ECG shows ST depression in V4–V6. She is hemodynamically stable.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for RWMA.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Lateral wall hypokinesis. Preserved global function. No effusion.
How does this change management? Lateral RWMA in the context of ST depression and chest pain is an NSTEMI with high-risk features. Activate the cath lab urgently. Anticoagulate. The echo finding corroborates the clinical diagnosis and raises urgency — do not wait for troponin results.



Case 4: Young patient with viral prodrome and shock
Clinical scenario: A 28-year-old man presents with 5 days of viral URI symptoms followed by 24 hours of progressive dyspnea and now hypotension (BP 88/60). He has no cardiac history.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Severely reduced EF. Globally hypokinetic but not dilated LV. No RWMA pattern. Small pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? Myocarditis with cardiogenic shock. This is not ischemic cardiomyopathy — no regional pattern, young patient, viral prodrome. Avoid NSAIDs (may worsen myocarditis). Start dobutamine. Urgent cardiology consultation for consideration of mechanical circulatory support — myocarditis-related shock can be rapidly fatal and some patients benefit from short-term MCS as a bridge to recovery. MRI is the gold standard for diagnosis but should not delay resuscitation.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. A hypotensive patient has a hyperdynamic LV on bedside echo. What does this tell you about the etiology of shock?






Caution





Answer Hyperdynamic LV function argues against cardiogenic shock as the primary etiology. Consider distributive shock (sepsis, anaphylaxis), hypovolemia, or obstructive shock. Mixed shock states are possible — a hyperdynamic LV does not guarantee adequate cardiac output if heart rate is severely elevated.



Q2. What is EPSS, and what does an elevated value indicate?






Caution





Answer E-point septal separation — the distance between the anterior mitral leaflet at its maximum opening excursion (E-point) and the interventricular septum, measured by M-mode on PLAX. Normal is less than 7 mm. Values above 7 mm correlate with reduced EF. It is a useful single-number surrogate when visual estimation is uncertain.



Q3. You see hypokinesis of the inferior wall and posterior wall on PSAX. What coronary territory does this implicate, and what additional structure should you assess?






Caution





Answer Right coronary artery (RCA) territory. Always assess the RV when inferior RWMA is present — the RCA supplies the RV free wall and an RCA occlusion can cause concomitant RV infarct. RV infarct requires volume loading and avoidance of nitrates, making it a distinct management scenario.



Q4. A patient has a severely reduced EF with a markedly dilated LV. A second patient has a severely reduced EF with a normal-sized LV. What does the difference in LV size suggest?






Caution





Answer Dilation suggests a chronic process — the heart has had time to remodel (dilated cardiomyopathy, longstanding ischemic disease). A non-dilated LV with severely reduced EF suggests an acute process: myocarditis, Takotsubo, acute large MI, or acute decompensation of previously compensated disease.



Q5. What is the Takotsubo pattern, and how does it differ from an LAD occlusion on bedside echo?






Caution





Answer Takotsubo (apical ballooning syndrome) shows apical and mid-ventricular hypokinesis or akinesis with preserved or hyperdynamic basal segments. An LAD occlusion causes anterior and apical dysfunction but typically includes some basal anterior involvement and follows the LAD distribution more closely. Takotsubo does not respect a single coronary territory — the basal sparing is the key distinguishing feature.

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Three questions in order.

Is there a pericardial effusion? An echo-free space surrounding the heart — confirmed in at least two views before acting on it.
Is it physiologically significant? Size alone does not determine significance. Look for chamber collapse, plethoric IVC, and respiratory variation — the hallmarks of elevated intrapericardial pressure.
Does this change what you do right now? Tamponade is a clinical and sonographic diagnosis. A large effusion in a hemodynamically stable patient may warrant monitoring and urgent cardiology consultation. The same effusion in a hypotensive patient with RA collapse is a needle emergency.



Pericardial ultrasound answers a binary, time-sensitive question at the bedside: does this patient need pericardiocentesis now? It also identifies effusions that will influence resuscitation strategy — for example, recognizing that aggressive fluid loading in tamponade provides only a brief bridge, and that vasopressors are a temporizing measure, not a solution. Getting the exam right means getting to the right intervention faster.

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a phased array (cardiac) probe for all windows. The footprint is small enough to fit between ribs, and the sector format gives the wide near-field view needed to see the full pericardium. If only a curvilinear probe is available, it is an acceptable substitute; a linear probe is not.
Set the machine to the cardiac preset — this inverts the color map convention and optimizes depth and gain for cardiac structures. Adjust depth so that the posterior pericardium is visible with a small margin beyond it; a common error is insufficient depth that clips the posterior effusion.


Subcostal four-chamber view






Tip



Video slot: Subcostal four-chamber acquisition — probe position, indicator orientation, fanning technique.


Probe placement: Subxiphoid, probe nearly flat against the abdomen (indicator to patient’s left, probe angle 15–20° above horizontal). Use the left lobe of the liver as an acoustic window.
How to optimize: Ask the patient to take a slow breath in and hold — this drops the diaphragm and brings the heart closer to the probe. Apply firm, steady pressure rather than jabbing. If the view is poor, try a more lateral subxiphoid position or ask the patient to bend their knees.
What you are looking for: All four chambers visible simultaneously, with the right ventricle nearest the probe. The pericardium appears as a bright echogenic line surrounding the heart. An effusion appears as an anechoic (black) stripe between the visceral and parietal pericardium.
Why this window first: In undifferentiated shock or cardiac arrest, the subcostal view is fastest to obtain and does not require repositioning. It is the window most likely to be achievable in a supine, ventilated patient.



Parasternal long axis






Tip



Video slot: Parasternal long axis acquisition — rib interspace selection, indicator to right shoulder, optimizing the view.


Probe placement: Left parasternal border, 3rd or 4th intercostal space, indicator pointing toward the patient’s right shoulder (roughly 10–11 o’clock). The left ventricle, mitral valve, aortic valve, left atrium, and proximal descending thoracic aorta are all visible in the same plane.
How to optimize: Move up or down one rib space if the view is cut off. Tilting the probe slightly lateral or medial adjusts the imaging plane through the long axis of the LV. The aortic valve should open symmetrically and the LV walls should appear equal in thickness.
What you are looking for: An effusion in PLAX appears as an echo-free stripe posterior to the LV, between the posterior LV wall and the pericardium. Key landmark: the descending thoracic aorta appears in cross-section at the far left of the image. Fluid anterior to the aorta is pericardial. Fluid posterior to the aorta is pleural. This distinction matters.



Apical four-chamber






Tip



Video slot: Apical four-chamber acquisition — point of maximal impulse, lateral decubitus positioning, depth and gain adjustments.


Probe placement: Point of maximal impulse (PMI), typically 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line. Indicator points to the patient’s left (3 o’clock). In obese patients or those with COPD, the PMI may be displaced; palpate for it rather than assuming position.
How to optimize: Left lateral decubitus positioning brings the heart toward the chest wall and dramatically improves image quality. Reduce depth so the apex is at the top of the screen (in cardiac convention, apex-up). Apical windows are often the most difficult — if the view is poor, try moving one interspace lateral or inferior.
What you are looking for: All four chambers, with the apex at top and the AV valves in the center. Effusion appears as echo-free space surrounding the heart. The apical view is particularly useful for identifying loculated effusions and for assessing respiratory variation across the mitral and tricuspid valves when tamponade physiology is suspected.

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
3. Normal & normal variants
The library of normal hearts and common confounders.
Fellows need to see ten or more normal studies before pathology is interpretable. The most common error is calling a normal structure an effusion — or missing a small effusion because the normal pericardium looks similar. Below are the key normals and variants to recognize.






Tip



Video slots: Normal studies across body habitus — lean, obese, COPD, post-CABG. Review each before proceeding to pathology.



Normal pericardium
The normal pericardium is a thin, bright (hyperechoic) line that moves with the heart. There is no echo-free space between the visceral and parietal layers in a normal study. A trace of fluid (up to 50 mL physiologically) may appear as a very thin stripe posteriorly on PLAX — this is normal and does not warrant intervention.


Pericardial fat pad
The most common mimic. Pericardial fat is echogenic (not echo-free), most prominent anteriorly, and does not shift with patient positioning. On subcostal view it appears as a bright, heterogeneous stripe anterior to the RV. Key distinguishing features:

Fat is echogenic; effusion is anechoic.
Fat does not change with the cardiac cycle; effusion may show swirling or layering.
Fat is anterior; hemodynamically significant effusions tend to be circumferential and posterior.



Epicardial fat
Epicardial fat sits between the myocardium and the visceral pericardium. It is visible as a thin echogenic layer, most prominent over the RV free wall and in the AV groove. It moves with the heart (unlike pericardial fat pad, which is relatively fixed). Distinguishing epicardial fat from a small effusion requires attention to echogenicity and motion.


Pleural effusion
A left pleural effusion appears posterior to the descending aorta on PLAX. Pericardial effusion appears anterior to the aorta. This landmark — the descending thoracic aorta — is the single most important landmark for distinguishing the two. Large left pleural effusions can also compress the heart and produce hemodynamic findings that mimic tamponade (so-called “pleural tamponade”).


Post-CABG appearance
After cardiac surgery, the pericardium is often left open or only partially closed. This creates an atypical pericardial appearance with adhesions, thickening, and potential for loculated collections. Post-operative effusions are frequently anterior and loculated — they may not be visible on subcostal view alone. The clinical context (recent sternotomy, new hemodynamic instability) should lower the threshold for a comprehensive multi-view exam or formal echo.

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding, not by diagnosis.

Small effusion






Tip



Video slot: Small posterior effusion on PLAX — thin echo-free stripe, preserved chamber function.


A small effusion is generally defined as less than 1 cm in greatest diameter on PLAX, posterior to the LV. It is visible in diastole and may disappear or thin in systole.
Teaching points:

Visible posteriorly first — the most dependent space when supine.
Does not produce chamber collapse.
Causes: pericarditis, viral illness, malignancy, uremia, post-procedure.
A small effusion in the right clinical context (chest pain, pleuritic quality, friction rub) supports the diagnosis of acute pericarditis and warrants NSAIDs and follow-up imaging, not pericardiocentesis.




Moderate to large effusion






Tip



Video slot: Large circumferential effusion — swinging heart, echo-free space in all windows.


Moderate: 1–2 cm; large: greater than 2 cm on PLAX. Large effusions are typically circumferential and visible in all windows.
Teaching points:

The “swinging heart” — pendular motion of the heart within a large effusion — is a classic finding and a marker of significant hemodynamic risk.
Size does not equal tamponade. A large chronic effusion (e.g., malignant) may be hemodynamically tolerated because the pericardium has had time to stretch. An acute effusion of even 200 mL (e.g., post-procedure, trauma) can cause tamponade because the pericardium has not had time to accommodate.
Always assess chamber collapse and IVC when a large effusion is present.




Tamponade physiology






Tip



Video slots:

RA free wall collapse in systole (subcostal or apical)
RV diastolic collapse (PLAX or subcostal)
Plethoric, non-collapsing IVC
Respiratory variation on mitral inflow (M-mode or PW Doppler)



Tamponade is elevated intrapericardial pressure exceeding intracardiac filling pressure. It is a clinical diagnosis confirmed sonographically. No single finding is pathognomonic — the diagnosis is integrative.
Sonographic findings, in order of sensitivity:








Finding
View
Notes




RA free wall collapse (systole)
Subcostal, apical
Earliest sign; sensitive but not specific


RV diastolic collapse
PLAX, subcostal
More specific; correlates with pressure equalization


Plethoric IVC (>2.1 cm, <50% collapse)
Subcostal IVC view
Reflects elevated right-sided filling pressures


Respiratory variation on mitral inflow >25%
Apical, PW Doppler
Sonographic equivalent of pulsus paradoxus



Management implication: When tamponade physiology is present in a hemodynamically unstable patient, the exam is over. Call for pericardiocentesis or emergent cardiothoracic surgery depending on the clinical context (medical vs. traumatic/surgical). Do not delay for formal echo.



Loculated effusion






Tip



Video slot: Post-operative loculated effusion — anterior, irregular, compressing RV.


Loculated effusions do not distribute freely around the heart. They occur after cardiac surgery, trauma, or prior pericarditis with adhesions. The collection may compress only one chamber, producing atypical hemodynamic presentations that do not fit classic tamponade physiology.
Teaching points:

Subcostal view may be normal; always check all windows.
Echogenic or heterogeneous fluid suggests blood, clot, or exudate.
Requires formal echo and cardiac surgery consultation — bedside pericardiocentesis is often not safe or effective for loculated collections.




Mimics & pitfalls







Mimic
Key distinguishing feature




Pleural effusion (left)
Posterior to descending aorta on PLAX


Pericardial fat pad
Echogenic, anterior, does not shift with positioning


Epicardial fat
Thin, moves with heart, between myocardium and visceral pericardium


Ascites
Seen in subcostal view, does not surround the heart


Right-sided pleural effusion
Visible lateral to RA/RV on subcostal; does not wrap posteriorly

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Post-procedure hypotension
Clinical scenario: A 68-year-old man undergoes a right heart catheterization for pulmonary hypertension workup. Thirty minutes after the procedure he is hypotensive (BP 82/50), tachycardic (HR 118), and mildly diaphoretic. He denies chest pain. The team is considering IV fluids and a vasopressor.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound, subcostal view first.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Large circumferential effusion. RA free wall collapses in systole. RV diastolic collapse present on subcostal and PLAX. IVC is 2.4 cm and non-collapsing.
How does this change management? Stop fluids — they will not correct tamponade. Call interventional cardiology and cardiac surgery simultaneously. Prepare for emergent pericardiocentesis. Do not start a vasopressor as the primary intervention; it temporizes without fixing the problem.



Case 2: Dyspnea in a cancer patient
Clinical scenario: A 54-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma presents with two weeks of worsening exertional dyspnea and a new feeling of fullness in her chest. BP 104/72, HR 102, RR 20. JVD is present. Chest X-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound — subcostal and PLAX minimum.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Very large circumferential effusion with swinging heart motion. No chamber collapse. IVC is 2.2 cm with minimal respiratory variation.
How does this change management? This patient is not in tamponade now but is at high risk. Oncology and cardiology consultation for semi-elective pericardiocentesis or pericardial window. Admit for monitoring. Do not discharge based on the absence of tamponade physiology at this moment — large malignant effusions can decompensate rapidly.



Case 3: Undifferentiated shock in the ED
Clinical scenario: A 44-year-old man arrives by EMS after being found unresponsive at home. BP 70/40, HR 124, GCS 10. No history available. He is cool, mottled, and has distended neck veins.
What exam would you perform? Immediate subcostal cardiac view as part of the resuscitation.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Moderate effusion. RA collapse in systole. No obvious RV collapse, but image quality is limited.
How does this change management? Activate the pericardiocentesis team. Limit IV fluids to one bolus as a bridge. Avoid deep sedation if intubation is needed — it can precipitate cardiac arrest in tamponade by eliminating sympathetic tone. If the patient arrests, perform pericardiocentesis before standard ACLS measures; defibrillation will not work if the heart cannot fill.



Case 4: Dialysis patient with chest pain
Clinical scenario: A 62-year-old man on hemodialysis three times weekly presents with sharp chest pain worse lying flat and better leaning forward. He missed his last two dialysis sessions. Vitals are stable. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for effusion and tamponade physiology.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Small-to-moderate posterior effusion. No chamber collapse. IVC is 2.5 cm (consistent with volume overload from missed dialysis).
How does this change management? Arrange urgent dialysis — this is the treatment for uremic pericarditis. NSAIDs are relatively contraindicated in ESRD. Admit for monitoring and repeat ultrasound after dialysis. Serial exams are appropriate — uremic effusions can enlarge rapidly if dialysis is delayed.



Case 5: Trauma — thoracic injury
Clinical scenario: A 29-year-old woman is brought in after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. She is intubated in the field. BP 88/60 on two vasopressors, HR 135. Bilateral breath sounds. No obvious external thoracic trauma.
What exam would you perform? FAST exam with focused cardiac view as the first priority.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Echo-free stripe anterior to the RV on subcostal view. RV diastolic collapse present. No obvious pleural effusions.
How does this change management? Emergent cardiothoracic surgery consultation. In a patient this unstable, pericardiocentesis alone is a bridge — the underlying injury requires operative repair. If the patient arrests, emergency department thoracotomy with pericardiotomy is indicated per ATLS protocol. Do not spend time on CT imaging.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis. The exam is a tool for action.

title: Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. On parasternal long axis, you see an echo-free space posterior to the LV. How do you determine whether it is pericardial or pleural?






Caution





Answer Locate the descending thoracic aorta in cross-section at the far left of the PLAX image. Fluid anterior to the aorta is pericardial. Fluid posterior to the aorta is pleural.



Q2. A patient has a large effusion and is hypotensive. You look for RV diastolic collapse but image quality is poor. What other findings support tamponade physiology?






Caution





Answer RA free wall collapse in systole (more sensitive, less specific), plethoric non-collapsing IVC (>2.1 cm, <50% inspiratory collapse), and respiratory variation on mitral inflow >25% by PW Doppler. No single finding is required — the diagnosis is integrative.



Q3. You see an echogenic structure anterior to the RV that does not move with the cardiac cycle. What is the most likely diagnosis, and how do you confirm it?






Caution





Answer Pericardial fat pad. Confirm by noting echogenicity (not echo-free), anterior location, and absence of positional shift. Reposition the patient — a true effusion will layer to the dependent position; fat will not.



Q4. A patient with known metastatic cancer has a large effusion but no chamber collapse. Is this patient safe for discharge?






Caution





Answer No. Absence of tamponade physiology at this moment does not mean it is safe to discharge. Large malignant effusions can decompensate rapidly. This patient needs admission, oncology and cardiology consultation, and a plan for drainage or a pericardial window.



Q5. In a trauma patient with tamponade physiology, why is pericardiocentesis alone often insufficient?






Caution





Answer Traumatic hemopericardium usually indicates a cardiac or great vessel injury. Pericardiocentesis may temporarily relieve pressure and buy time, but the underlying structural injury requires operative repair. Definitive management is in the operating room.

title: Module 3 — Right Ventricular Function
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Two questions in order.

Is the RV dilated or failing? A visually enlarged RV — approaching or exceeding the size of the LV — is the primary finding. Normal RV is roughly two-thirds the size of the LV on apical four-chamber view.
What is the cause, and does it require immediate intervention? RV failure from massive PE is a needle/catheter emergency. RV failure from chronic pulmonary hypertension or ARDS needs a different approach. The echo does not always give you the diagnosis — it gives you the hemodynamic phenotype to guide management.



The RV is the chamber most often underappreciated in critical care. It operates as a low-pressure, high-compliance structure that tolerates volume overload relatively well but is exquisitely sensitive to acute pressure increases. When RV afterload rises acutely — as in massive PE — the RV dilates rapidly, shifts the interventricular septum, impairs LV filling, and drives the patient into obstructive shock. Recognizing this pattern quickly and accurately is one of the highest-yield skills in critical care echo.

text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a phased array (cardiac) probe on the cardiac preset. RV assessment requires at least two views. The apical four-chamber is the primary window; PSAX at the mid-ventricular level provides the D-sign. Subcostal is the fallback in unstable patients.


Apical four-chamber






Tip



Video slot: Apical four-chamber for RV assessment — RV:LV ratio, free wall motion, TAPSE measurement.


What you are looking for: RV size relative to the LV. The RV free wall should move briskly inward in systole. TAPSE (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion) is measured by M-mode at the lateral tricuspid annulus — normal is greater than 17 mm. Reduced TAPSE indicates RV systolic dysfunction regardless of the cause.
Avoid the pitfall: The apical view can foreshorten the LV and artificially make the RV appear larger. If the RV appears large, confirm in a second window.



Parasternal short axis — mid-ventricular level






Tip



Video slot: PSAX for D-sign — normal circular LV vs pressure-overloaded D-shape.


What you are looking for: The LV should appear round (like a donut) in cross-section throughout the cardiac cycle. When RV pressure or volume overload is present, the interventricular septum flattens or bows toward the LV, creating a D-shaped LV.

Septal flattening in systole: RV pressure overload (PE, pulmonary hypertension)
Septal flattening in diastole: RV volume overload
Septal flattening throughout: both




Parasternal long axis — RV outflow






Tip



Video slot: PLAX with attention to RV — RV dilation encroaching on the LV, RVOT assessment.


What you are looking for: RV free wall thickness (normal <5 mm; >5 mm suggests chronic pressure overload), RVOT dilation, and subjective assessment of RV size relative to LVOT.



Subcostal






Tip



Video slot: Subcostal view for RV — free wall, size assessment, RV-to-LV comparison.


When to use: First-line in the peri-arrest or ventilated patient. The subcostal view shows the RV nearest the probe and allows rapid assessment of RV size and free wall motion.

title: Module 3 — Right Ventricular Function
text:
3. Normal & normal variants






Tip



Video slots: Normal RV in apical four-chamber — thin free wall, RV smaller than LV, brisk TAPSE. Compare with RV in an athletic heart (mild physiologic enlargement).



Normal RV size and function
On apical four-chamber, the RV should occupy roughly the right one-third of the image and appear clearly smaller than the LV. The RV free wall is thin and moves vigorously. TAPSE is greater than 17 mm. Normal RV wall thickness on subcostal is less than 5 mm.


Physiologic RV enlargement
Highly trained athletes may have mildly enlarged RVs — a normal variant without functional impairment. TAPSE and free wall motion remain normal. Clinical context distinguishes this from pathologic enlargement.


RV hypertrophy
Free wall thickness greater than 5 mm indicates chronic pressure overload. The RV has remodeled over time. Seen in chronic pulmonary hypertension, severe COPD, and longstanding left heart disease. A hypertrophied RV tolerates acute pressure increases somewhat better than a normal-thickness RV, which is why patients with chronic PHT may tolerate elevated PA pressures that would immediately cause acute cor pulmonale in a previously healthy patient.

title: Module 3 — Right Ventricular Function
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding, not by diagnosis.

RV dilation






Tip



Video slot: Dilated RV on apical four-chamber — RV approaching or exceeding LV size.


RV:LV ratio approaching 1:1 or greater on apical four-chamber is abnormal. The RV free wall may still contract (compensated) or may be hypokinetic (decompensated).
Teaching points:

Acute dilation without free wall hypertrophy = acute process (PE, acute cor pulmonale from ARDS, RV infarct).
Dilation with free wall hypertrophy = chronic process (pulmonary hypertension, COPD).
The acuity of onset changes the differential and the urgency of intervention.




D-sign (septal flattening)






Tip



Video slots: - D-sign from pressure overload (systolic flattening) — PE, PHT - D-sign from volume overload (diastolic flattening) — TR, ASD


The interventricular septum flattens or bows toward the LV due to elevated RV pressure or volume. The timing within the cardiac cycle distinguishes pressure from volume overload.
Teaching points:

Septal shift impairs LV filling (ventricular interdependence) and can cause hypotension even with a structurally normal LV.
The D-sign is most reliably assessed on PSAX.
In mechanical ventilation, the D-sign may be accentuated by high PEEP and should be interpreted in clinical context.




McConnell’s sign






Tip



Video slot: McConnell’s sign — RV free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing (apical flicking).


Regional RV dysfunction with akinesis of the mid-free wall and preserved or hyperdynamic motion at the RV apex. Originally described as specific for acute PE (specificity ~94%, sensitivity ~77%). The mechanism is thought to involve tethering of the RV apex to the contracting LV.
Teaching points:

Highly specific for acute PE when present, but absence does not rule out PE.
Can be seen in other conditions causing acute RV pressure overload.
In the right clinical context (tachycardia, hypoxia, plethoric IVC), McConnell’s sign is enough to initiate PE workup and consider empiric thrombolytics in an unstable patient.




Reduced TAPSE






Tip



Video slot: TAPSE measurement by M-mode — normal vs reduced.


TAPSE below 17 mm indicates RV systolic dysfunction. It reflects longitudinal RV function and correlates with prognosis across multiple conditions including PE, pulmonary hypertension, and right heart failure.
Teaching points:

TAPSE is load-dependent — it can be reduced in hypovolemia and improved with volume loading.
A TAPSE of 10 mm in a patient who was normal yesterday represents a severe acute event.
Serial TAPSE measurement tracks RV recovery in response to treatment.




Mimics & pitfalls







Pitfall
Explanation




Foreshortened apical view
Makes RV appear artificially large; confirm in a second window


Anterior MI with RV involvement
RV dilation from infarct, not PE — ECG and clinical context distinguish


Athletic heart
Mild RV enlargement without functional impairment


High PEEP
Can cause RV dilation and D-sign independent of intrinsic RV pathology


RBBB
Can cause apparent septal dyskinesis on echo unrelated to pressure overload

title: Module 3 — Right Ventricular Function
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Massive PE — hemodynamic collapse
Clinical scenario: A 55-year-old man on a long-haul flight arrives at a connecting airport and collapses in the terminal. He is brought to the ED with BP 70/40, HR 130, O2 saturation 84% on non-rebreather. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with right heart strain pattern (S1Q3T3).
What exam would you perform? Immediate subcostal cardiac view and IVC.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Massively dilated RV, RV:LV ratio >1. McConnell’s sign present. D-sign on PSAX. Plethoric, non-collapsing IVC. No pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? This is massive PE with obstructive shock. The echo is sufficient to act — do not wait for CT. Administer systemic thrombolytics (tPA 100 mg over 2 hours or 50 mg bolus if arrest is imminent) unless there is a hard contraindication. If contraindicated, activate interventional radiology or cardiac surgery for catheter-directed therapy or surgical embolectomy. Avoid large fluid boluses — the dilated RV cannot accommodate more volume and fluids may worsen septal shift and LV underfilling.



Case 2: Submassive PE — how sick is this RV?
Clinical scenario: A 42-year-old woman presents with 3 days of pleuritic chest pain and progressive dyspnea. BP 108/72, HR 105, O2 saturation 92% on room air. CT confirms bilateral PE with clot in the main pulmonary arteries. Troponin is positive.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess RV function and guide risk stratification.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Mildly to moderately dilated RV. RV free wall hypokinesis present. No McConnell’s sign. TAPSE 12 mm. D-sign on PSAX. LV filling appears reduced.
How does this change management? This is submassive (intermediate-high risk) PE with echo evidence of RV dysfunction and myocardial injury (elevated troponin). Anticoagulate immediately. The RV dysfunction on echo upgrades risk and supports consideration of early catheter-directed therapy rather than anticoagulation alone. Admit to a monitored setting. Serial echo is appropriate to track RV recovery.



Case 3: ARDS and RV failure
Clinical scenario: A 67-year-old man with severe ARDS (P:F ratio 90) is on lung-protective ventilation with PEEP 16 and FiO2 0.80. He is increasingly vasopressor-dependent on day 3 of his ICU course. No new fever or culture data.
What exam would you perform? Bedside cardiac ultrasound to assess for ventilator-induced cor pulmonale.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: RV dilated, RV:LV ratio 0.9. D-sign present throughout the cardiac cycle. TAPSE 13 mm. No McConnell’s sign. Plethoric IVC.
How does this change management? Acute cor pulmonale from ARDS. High PEEP increases RV afterload; hypercapnia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction and worsens it further. Interventions: reduce PEEP if oxygenation allows, target normocapnia, consider prone positioning (reduces RV afterload and improves V/Q matching), inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (inhaled NO or epoprostenol) to reduce RV afterload. Avoid further fluid loading.



Case 4: RV infarct
Clinical scenario: A 70-year-old man with an inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF) is being transferred for primary PCI. His BP is 82/54 and HR 88. He received sublingual nitroglycerin in the field and his BP dropped to 60 systolic briefly.
What exam would you perform? Rapid focused cardiac echo before transfer.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Inferior and posterior wall hypokinesis (LV). RV free wall hypokinesis. RV mildly dilated. LV function otherwise preserved.
How does this change management? RV infarct complicating inferior STEMI. Nitroglycerin is contraindicated — it reduces preload and the failing RV is entirely preload-dependent. Administer IV fluid bolus (500 mL) to maintain RV filling pressure. Avoid diuretics. Maintain AV synchrony — loss of atrial kick is poorly tolerated. Expedite PCI — reperfusion of the RCA is the treatment.






Tip

Quiz

Note



Q1. On apical four-chamber, the RV appears as large as the LV. What is your next step before concluding RV dilation is present?






Caution





Answer Confirm in a second window. The apical view can foreshorten the LV and artificially make the RV appear large. PSAX or subcostal view should confirm the finding before acting on it.



Q2. The D-sign is present in systole but resolves in diastole on PSAX. What does this pattern indicate?






Caution





Answer Systolic septal flattening indicates RV pressure overload — the RV systolic pressure is elevated above normal (e.g., massive PE, acute pulmonary hypertension). Diastolic flattening indicates volume overload. Flattening throughout the cycle suggests combined pressure and volume overload.



Q3. What is McConnell’s sign and what condition is it most associated with?






Caution





Answer McConnell’s sign is akinesis of the RV mid-free wall with preserved or hyperdynamic motion at the RV apex. It is most associated with acute pulmonary embolism (specificity ~94%). The mechanism involves tethering of the RV apex to the contracting LV apex through shared myocardial fibers.



Q4. A patient with massive PE and obstructive shock has a BP of 68/40. Why should you avoid large fluid boluses?






Caution





Answer The RV is already severely distended. Additional volume causes further RV dilation, worsens D-sign and septal shift, reduces LV diastolic filling, and drops cardiac output further. A small bolus (250–500 mL) may be given as a bridge, but the primary intervention is restoring RV afterload reduction through thrombolysis or mechanical reperfusion.



Q5. TAPSE is measured at 10 mm in a patient with known chronic pulmonary hypertension. How does this differ from the same TAPSE in a patient who was normal yesterday?






Caution





Answer In chronic PHT, a TAPSE of 10 mm may represent stable (if severely impaired) chronic RV dysfunction. In a previously normal patient, TAPSE of 10 mm represents acute, severe RV failure — the RV has not had time to compensate and the patient is at immediate risk of hemodynamic collapse. Acute RV failure is a medical emergency; chronic RV dysfunction requires optimization but is not immediately life-threatening in the same way.

title: Module 5 — IVC & Volume Status
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Two questions in order.

Is this patient likely to respond to a fluid bolus? A collapsible, small IVC in a spontaneously breathing patient suggests low right-sided filling pressure and likely fluid responsiveness. A plethoric, non-collapsing IVC suggests elevated venous pressure — giving fluid will not help and may cause harm.
Is there venous congestion? An elevated IVC diameter with loss of respiratory variation, combined with hepatic vein dilation and portal vein pulsatility, indicates systemic venous hypertension. This pattern shifts the frame from “give fluid” to “treat the cause of congestion.”



The IVC is the most accessible venous structure for bedside hemodynamic assessment. It is also the most misused. A collapsible IVC does not guarantee that a fluid bolus will improve cardiac output — it indicates that the right atrial pressure is low, which is one of several conditions necessary for fluid responsiveness. Equally important, a plethoric IVC is not always tamponade — it can reflect right heart failure, PE, severe tricuspid regurgitation, or aggressive fluid resuscitation. The IVC is one data point in a hemodynamic assessment, not a standalone decision-maker.
